issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'full sensory reliving' suggests highly vivid, poorly contextualized trauma memory, which sits in marked tension with 'I can talk about what happened very easily.' Those two can sometimes coexist, but as a three-item profile with shame on recall they pull in opposing directions and are clinically questionable together.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: 'Avoid enclosed spaces' is not clearly coherent with the rest of the profile for sexual assault as described here. The threat and memory items center on being followed, danger in unfamiliar places, delays, shame, and vivid reliving; enclosed spaces introduces a more specific situational avoidance that is not supported by the memory/threat content and looks disconnected from the formulation, especially since Triggers is not active in this case.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' sits in tension with 'When I remember the event I feel intense shame' and 'Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time.' Severe shame and terror on recall usually make disclosure difficult rather than easy, so this combination is clinically questionable within the same node.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant
issues.explanation: 'Ruminate about how to get even with assailant' is a poor fit with the rest of the profile for this trauma type and patient presentation. The Memory and Threat items emphasize shame, terror, hypervigilance, and avoidance, which is more consistent with fear-based post-assault PTSD; revenge-focused rumination pulls toward a different emotional/cognitive stance and lacks support elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement
issues.explanation: 'Gambling' is not impossible, but in this profile it is weakly anchored to the rest of the presentation. The dominant active formulation is Memory↔Threat↔Maladaptive Strategies around trauma recollection and danger monitoring after sexual assault; gambling for excitement/distracting oneself is too nonspecific and does not connect clearly to the patient's other selected threat and memory items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Enclosed Spaces: Enclosed or confined spaces
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Enclosed Spaces' appears to be a trigger/avoidance cue rather than a maladaptive strategy, and it is poorly matched to the rest of the profile. The threat and memory items center on being followed, danger in unfamiliar places, shame, terror, and speechless recall; avoidance of enclosed spaces is a different contextual pattern that is not otherwise supported here.

vignette: Michael, a 53-year-old married social worker from North American descent, has been struggling with intrusive thoughts and avoidance behaviors following a traumatic sexual assault that occurred several months ago. The incident left him feeling vulnerable and triggered intense feelings of shame and terror whenever he recalled it. The night of the assault was particularly harrowing for Michael. It happened while he was walking home late one evening from a community event at a local park. As he turned down a dimly lit alleyway, an unknown assailant ambushed him, overpowering him with a knife and forcing him into a nearby storage shed. The enclosed space made his helplessness all the more palpable, and the assault left him feeling violated and stripped of control. Since that night, Michael has been unable to enter any enclosed or confined spaces without experiencing severe anxiety and flashbacks. He had come to believe that being in such environments would inevitably trigger memories of the attack. This avoidance extended to his work as a social worker where he often needed to meet clients in small offices within community centers. As a result, Michael started scheduling meetings outdoors or in open areas whenever possible, which led to some delays and misunderstandings with colleagues who found it strange that their regular appointments kept changing locations. Michael's thoughts about the assault consumed him constantly, and he frequently ruminated on how to get even with his assailant. He tried pushing these thoughts out of his mind but often found himself spiraling into dark scenarios where he imagined confronting and punishing the person responsible for his trauma. This relentless cycle only increased his anxiety and made it difficult for him to focus on work or home life. When something took longer than expected, Michael assumed the worst, feeling that danger was imminent. His wife noticed a significant change in his behavior; he would frequently check behind him as if expecting someone to follow him. The uncertainty about whether he was safe became overwhelming, and he began avoiding unfamiliar places altogether. This avoidance extended even to familiar environments where he felt uncertain of the layout or security measures. Recalling the assault brought back intense feelings of shame and terror for Michael. Whenever these memories surfaced, he found it difficult to articulate what had happened, often feeling like the words failed him when trying to describe his experience. He was certain that expressing such vulnerability would only deepen his sense of humiliation and inadequacy. These symptoms have taken a toll on his personal life as well. His wife grew concerned about his increasing isolation and reluctance to engage in activities they both used to enjoy together, like dining out or attending social gatherings. Their relationship began to feel strained by Michael's withdrawal and avoidance behaviors, leading to moments of tension and misunderstanding between them. Finally, the weight of his symptoms became too much for Michael to bear on his own. He realized that he needed professional help to navigate through these overwhelming feelings and regain control over his life. His greatest fear was being vulnerable again, but he also hoped that therapy would provide him with tools to manage his anxiety and reclaim a sense of normalcy in his daily life. Michael is now seeking help not just for himself but also to salvage the relationships and work environment that have been impacted by his trauma. He hopes to find ways to confront his fears without being overwhelmed by them, ultimately regaining a sense of security and control over his life.
